text: PASSAGE (SRC-02-P1): A vaccine works less like a medicine and more like a rehearsal. Instead of attacking an infection directly, it presents the body with a harmless version of a germ, or merely a fragment of one, so that the immune system can study it in advance. Certain white blood cells respond by producing antibodies shaped to fit that particular invader, while others, known as memory cells, keep a record of the encounter for years. If the real germ arrives later, the body recognises it quickly and mounts a defence before serious illness can take hold. This explains why a vaccine against one disease offers no help against another: the training is highly specific. It also explains why some vaccines need booster doses, since the memory of certain germs fades with time. The approach has limits. Germs that change their outer coat rapidly can slip past an old memory, which is why some vaccines must be updated regularly. Even so, the principle remains remarkably economical. By teaching the body to defend itself, a small dose given in advance can prevent suffering that no treatment afterwards could fully undo. || Which of the following is the most appropriate title for the passage?

text: PASSAGE (SRC-02-P2): For many coastal towns, the first response to rising seas and stronger storms has been to build higher walls. A sea wall is visible, easy to explain and quick to approve, and it can protect a harbour or a busy road for decades. subject: Reading Comprehension
text: PASSAGE (SRC-02-P3): Waiting is usually described as wasted time, the empty stretch between one useful activity and the next. A passenger on a delayed train checks the clock again and again, and every minute seems longer than the last. Yet the same minutes pass quite differently for a child waiting for a festival or a farmer waiting for the rains. What changes is not the length of time but our relation to it. When we cannot see an end, or feel that someone else controls it, waiting becomes a burden; when we know why we wait and trust that the wait will be rewarded, it can feel like part of the event itself. Several traditions have treated patience as a skill rather than a mere absence of action. This does not mean that every delay deserves acceptance; a wait caused by carelessness should be corrected rather than admired.
